notes.b: Hormones are chemical messengers that control growth and body functions. Because they act in tiny amounts, people can change how an organism works by adding hormones or blocking them. This is called hormonal manipulation, and it is used in sport, health and agriculture.
points: Hormonal manipulation is the deliberate use of natural or synthetic (man-made) hormones, or of drugs that block hormones, to change how an organism grows or functions.
It can work by adding a hormone the body lacks or by supplying extra, or by blocking a hormone's release or action, so the body's own control system is deliberately altered.
The syllabus asks you to recognise the impact of these manipulations on organisms, so for each use you need the benefit and the cost.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one use of hormones in each of sport, medicine and agriculture, so learn at least one clear example from each area.

notes.b: Some athletes take hormones to gain a physical edge. Two are misused: anabolic steroids, which build muscle, and EPO, which boosts the blood's oxygen supply. Both are dangerous and banned.
points: Anabolic steroids are synthetic derivatives of testosterone (the male sex hormone). They increase muscle mass and strength and speed up recovery from training, which is why athletes misuse them.
Anabolic steroids cause liver damage, increase the risk of heart disease, and cause acne and mood changes including aggression.
In males, anabolic steroids reduce sperm production, cause infertility and cause shrinking of the testes.
In females, anabolic steroids cause male characteristics to develop, because the drug is a form of a male hormone.
EPO (erythropoietin) is a hormone made by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell production.
Athletes misuse EPO to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, because red blood cells carry oxygen, and so their endurance.
Extra red cells thicken the blood, which increases the risk of clots, heart attack and stroke.
The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) bans these substances in competitive sport and tests athletes through urine and blood samples. Their use is unfair to other competitors.
notes.tip: If asked why steroids or EPO are banned, give two reasons: the health risks (name a side effect) and the unfair advantage over other competitors.

notes.b: Doctors use hormones to replace ones the body no longer makes enough of, to control fertility and to relieve symptoms of ageing. Each treatment fixes a specific hormone problem.
points: Insulin injections treat type 1 diabetes, in which the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so blood glucose would otherwise rise too high.
Most insulin used today is human insulin made by genetically modified bacteria (bacteria given the human insulin gene). There is more on this in Genetic Engineering.
The contraceptive pill contains synthetic oestrogen and progesterone, or progesterone alone. These are female sex hormones.
The pill inhibits (reduces) the release of FSH and LH, the pituitary hormones that make an egg mature and be released, so no egg matures and ovulation (release of an egg) is prevented.
Fertility treatment uses hormones to stimulate the ovaries to release eggs, which helps women who do not ovulate normally to become pregnant.

Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) supplies oestrogen, often with progesterone, after the menopause (when the ovaries stop producing these hormones) to relieve symptoms such as hot flushes and to reduce bone loss.
For some women, HRT slightly increases the risk of some cancers and of blood clots, so it carries a risk as well as a benefit.
Thyroxine tablets are given to people whose thyroid gland produces too little thyroxine, replacing the missing hormone.
notes.tip: To explain how the pill works, name FSH and LH, say their release is inhibited, then link this to no egg maturing and no ovulation. For HRT, say the risk applies to some women, not all.

notes.b: Farmers use hormones to control breeding, boost yields and manage plants. Animal uses raise welfare and food-safety concerns, while plant hormones are used as weedkillers, rooting aids and ripening agents.
points: Progesterone, given as a vaginal sponge or implant, synchronises the breeding cycles of cattle and sheep, so a herd can be bred and give birth at the same time.
Growth-promoting hormones increase meat production in cattle.
Bovine somatotropin (BST), a growth hormone from cattle, increases milk yield in cattle.
Growth-promoting hormones and BST are banned in the EU, including Ireland, because of concerns about animal welfare and hormone residues (traces left behind) in food. BST is permitted in the USA.
Synthetic auxins such as 2,4-D are selective weedkillers (they kill some plants but not others). They kill broad-leaved weeds in cereal crops by making them grow uncontrollably.
Auxin rooting powder makes cuttings (pieces cut from a plant) form roots, so new plants can be grown from them.
Ethene gas is used to ripen fruit such as bananas in storage after transport, so fruit can be shipped unripe and ripened when needed.
notes.tip: Give only the uses of plant hormones here, not how they control normal growth. For hormones in food production, say what is gained and why the EU bans some.

notes.b: Hormonal manipulation brings real gains but also real harms. To evaluate it, weigh the benefits against the costs for each use.
points: Benefits: better health, treatment of disease (such as insulin for type 1 diabetes), increased food production and convenience (such as synchronised breeding and ripening on demand).
Costs: side effects (such as those of anabolic steroids, EPO and HRT), an unfair advantage in sport, animal welfare concerns, hormone residues in food and environmental effects of weedkillers.
notes.tip: When asked to evaluate hormones in food production, give at least one benefit and one cost, such as higher meat or milk yield against welfare concerns and residues in food.

questions.prompt: Give one example of the use of hormones in each of sport, health and agriculture, and explain the purpose of each.
questions.model: Sport: anabolic steroids, which are synthetic testosterone, increase muscle mass and strength and speed up recovery from training. Or EPO, which is made by the kidneys and stimulates red blood cell production, is used to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and so endurance. Health: insulin injections treat type 1 diabetes, where the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so blood glucose is controlled. Or the contraceptive pill, containing synthetic oestrogen and progesterone, inhibits the release of FSH and LH so that ovulation is prevented. Agriculture: progesterone is used to synchronise the breeding cycles of cattle and sheep so that a herd gives birth at the same time. Or synthetic auxin 2,4-D is used as a selective weedkiller to kill broad-leaved weeds in cereal crops. Or ethene gas is used to ripen fruit such as bananas in storage.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of hormones in sport.
questions.model: Benefits: anabolic steroids increase muscle mass and strength and speed up recovery from training, and EPO increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, improving endurance. Costs: anabolic steroids cause liver damage, increase the risk of heart disease, reduce sperm production and infertility in males, cause male characteristics in females, acne and mood changes including aggression. EPO thickens the blood, increasing the risk of clots, heart attack and stroke. Their use is unfair to other competitors, so the World Anti-Doping Agency bans them in competitive sport and tests athletes through urine and blood samples. On balance, the health risks and the unfair advantage outweigh the benefits, which is why these hormones are banned.
